# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the margins, noticed by no one, significant to no one, yet somehow constituting the actual texture of existence. This thought came to me last Tuesday while watching a pigeon navigate a parking lot—not a dramatic observation, not something that would impress anyone at dinner, but the kind of small attention that seems increasingly rare.

We live in an age of curated significance. Everything worth noticing has already been noticed, packaged, and presented to us through screens. We consume these pre-digested observations and call ourselves informed. Meanwhile, the actual world—messy, redundant, ungainly—continues its work unobserved. I find something deeply moving about this. It suggests that beneath the layers of attention we've collectively decided to pay to major events and carefully crafted content, there exists an entire parallel universe of unremarkable things, simply existing, asking nothing of us.

That pigeon, for instance. I watched it for perhaps three minutes while waiting for someone at a coffee shop. It was engaged in what I can only describe as aggressive optimization—attempting to navigate around a puddle, reconsidering, trying another route, eventually just walking through the puddle with obvious irritation, as if the water had personally offended it. I found myself wondering whether pigeons have the capacity to be annoyed, whether what I was interpreting as annoyance was something else entirely, or whether, in fact, this particular pigeon was simply executing a series of mechanical responses and I was projecting an entire inner life onto a bird that probably didn't have one.

This is the fundamental problem with noticing: it immediately leads to interpretation, and interpretation leads to stories, and stories are where we lose the thing itself.

But I'm interested in stories anyway. I'm interested in the stories we tell ourselves about what we notice, because those stories might be more true, in some meaningful sense, than the raw facts. If I'm the only person who watched that pigeon, and I watched it with the genuine attention that most people reserve for their phones, didn't I create something real? Wasn't there a small event—a pigeon noticing, witnessed—that didn't exist before?

This connects to something I've been reading about attention as a moral act. The idea that there is something almost sacred about genuine attention—the kind where you're not performing attention for some audience, not scrolling while pretending to listen, but actually there, actually present with the thing in front of you. This kind of attention has become so rare that I wonder if we should coin a new word for it, something with more weight than "attention," which has been so depleted by overuse that it barely means anything anymore.

I've noticed that the people I most enjoy talking to are the ones who practice this kind of attention. Not in a performative way—they're not being "mindful" or "present" with the self-conscious intensity of someone trying to prove something. Rather, they simply seem to be genuinely interested in what's in front of them, including conversations. When you're talking to someone like this, you can feel it. It's a rare sensation, this experience of being fully attended to. We're so starved for it that when it happens, we often mistake it for romance or special connection, when sometimes it's just someone actually listening.

I've also noticed that attention is contagious. When you really look at something, other people start to look too. I remember once, years ago, stopping in the middle of a busy street because I'd seen something—I can't even remember what now, some configuration of light or color—and within thirty seconds, three other people had stopped beside me wondering what I was looking at. We all stood there staring at whatever it was, strangers united in curiosity, and I felt a genuine sense of community in that moment. The spell broke when someone asked "what are we looking at?" and we all realized we couldn't quite articulate it, so we laughed and moved on. But something real had happened.

There's a particular kind of boredom that I think is valuable, though it's almost extinct now. It's the boredom you experience when you're not allowed to use your phone, not in any social punishment sense, but just in normal daily life. Walking somewhere without music, waiting for someone without scrolling, sitting in a quiet room without entertainment. In these moments, boredom used to lead to observation. Your brain, desperate for stimulus, would start really noticing things. The cracks in the pavement. The way light falls through a window. The small social dramas unfolding around you.

I've been deliberately creating these moments lately, and I've found it surprisingly difficult. My instinct, trained by years of constant stimulus availability, is to reach for my phone the moment I'm not actively engaged with something. When I manage to resist this instinct, there's usually a grace period of acute discomfort—fifteen seconds, sometimes thirty—where I feel genuinely anxious. Then it passes, and I start to notice things again. It's like my attention apparatus has to be rebooted each time.

One thing I've noticed is how many small kindnesses happen invisibly. A person holding a door even though the person behind them is still far enough away that they're going to have to hold it for an awkward amount of time. Someone picking up a dropped glove and looking around to find the owner, with zero chance of recognition or thanks. A barista remembering how someone likes their coffee. These are not the kind of things that appear on social media, not because they're not good, but because they're not performed. There's something about the invisible kindness that makes it purer, less corrupted by the possibility of external reward.

I wonder if this is why so many people feel an emptiness even when everything in their lives appears, by reasonable metrics, to be going well. We're optimizing for visibility rather than quality. We're curating our lives for an imaginary audience that doesn't actually exist, or if it does, doesn't actually care as much as we think. The parts of life that are most meaningful—the small moments of genuine connection, the quiet satisfaction of doing something well with no one watching, the strange peace of being alone without being lonely—these aren't on our résumés. They don't show up in photos. They're the stuff that life is made of, and we're training ourselves to overlook them.

There's also something interesting about the specific ways that people develop their own noticing patterns. We don't all notice the same things. Some people are extremely attuned to others' emotional states, picking up on microexpressions and tone shifts that completely escape me. Other people notice architectural details or bird species or the mechanical consistency of a well-made object. I've found that I notice patterns of behavior, the way people handle small frustrations, the revealed preferences in how people talk about their days.

This might be why conversations are so valuable—because each person brings a different quality of attention to the world, and when you really listen to someone talk about what they've noticed, you get to borrow their attention apparatus for a while. You get to see the world through their particular filter. A friend who notices birds can take you on a walk and transform it into a completely different experience than you would have had alone. Another friend might make you acutely aware of the emotional dynamics at a party you might have thought was fine.

The problem, of course, is that we have less time for this kind of conversation now. We have more "connections" but less deep attention within those connections. We're all rushing toward the next thing, the next notification, the next stimulus. The paradox is that by trying to maximize experiences, we're minimizing the quality of attention we can bring to any given experience. We're trying to taste all the wines, and in doing so, we're not really tasting any of them.

I've started a small practice of what I'm calling "mandatory noticing." Once a day, usually while I'm out somewhere, I pick something and really look at it—not for any purpose, not to write about it or post about it or tell anyone about it, just to see it clearly. It's harder than it sounds. My mind keeps trying to turn the observation into something—a thought, a story, a photograph. I have to keep gently bringing it back to the simple act of looking.

Some of these observations are beautiful. A garden in someone's front yard where you can see exactly which plants are getting adequate light and which are struggling. The way a particular tree grows, all its limbs reaching toward one side because of how the surrounding buildings block the light. A storefront window display that's obviously been arranged by someone with specific aesthetics and taste.

But some of them are mundane in a way that's almost meditative. The texture of a wall. The pattern of cracks in concrete. A pile of leaves in a corner. The accumulated grime on a streetlight. These things are not beautiful, but they are real in a way that curated images are not. They are the actual world, unarranged, unfiltered, indifferent to whether anyone notices.

And I think that indifference might be important. In a world where everything is increasingly personalized, where algorithms learn our preferences and serve us more of the same, there's something grounding about things that simply exist without any reference to us. A tree doesn't know you're looking at it. A pigeon doesn't care whether you think it's annoyed. The world was here before you paid attention to it, and it will continue after you stop. There's something reassuring about this.

I don't have any grand conclusions here. I'm not suggesting that everyone should practice mandatory noticing or that attention is the solution to all modern malaise. But I do think there's something we're losing by outsourcing our noticing to algorithms and curators. We're losing touch with the irreplaceable experience of being a conscious creature in a world full of things worth paying attention to.

The pigeon probably never appears in anyone else's story. It navigated its parking lot, found what it was looking for or didn't, and moved on, completely indifferent to the fact that someone was watching. But for those three minutes, it was the entire world—the only thing happening that mattered. And I think we need more moments like that, moments where the entire world shrinks down to whatever is directly in front of us, and we're content to simply notice.
